title: A Fear-Driven King
sum: Exodus begins where Genesis ended: Jacob's seventy descendants in Egypt, Joseph dead, and a family that has become a people. They "were fruitful and swarmed," words from the creation story. A new king who "did not know Joseph" sees their numbers as a threat. He forces them into gang labor building the supply cities Pithom and Rameses, and the more he crushes them, the more they grow.

When forced labor fails, Pharaoh orders two Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill newborn boys. They fear God more than the king, and God rewards them. Pharaoh's last order is open genocide: every newborn son must be thrown into the Nile. The chapter names the midwives but never the king.
readings: Read as history

A people of Semitic origin living in the eastern Delta is drafted for royal building. Egyptian sources do show Asiatic workers making bricks, quotas, and cities called Pi-Ramesses and Per-Atum. Traditional readers take the chapter as the start of a real oppression, whose king is usually named as Thutmose I or III (early date) or Seti I or Ramesses II (late date).
Read as literature

The chapter is a reversal of Genesis. Creation words ("fruitful," "multiply," "filled the land") describe Israel, and Pharaoh plays the role of chaos, trying to undo that blessing. Water, the means of his decree, will become the means of his defeat. The two women who defy him are the first of several women who save Moses.
Read as liberation

For enslaved Africans in America, Latin American Christians and many others, this chapter named their own experience: forced labor, fear of a growing minority, and violence against children. Michael Walzer called the exodus the West's master story of revolution: from oppression, through the wilderness, to a promised land.

views.H: A historical oppression in the New Kingdom. Pithom and Rameses fit the eastern Delta, and Egyptian records of brickmaking quotas and Asiatic laborers support the setting. Defenders of the 1446 BC date take "Rameses" as a later name for an older site.
views.M: A smaller group, perhaps the ancestors of the Levites, really was enslaved in the Delta; several Levite names are Egyptian (Moses, Phinehas, Hophni). Their memory of forced labor became the shared memory of all Israel.
views.C: No Egyptian text mentions Israel in Egypt. The story draws on general memories of Semites in the Delta, the expulsion of the Hyksos, and Egyptian rule over Canaan, and shapes them into a national origin story. The city names and details fit the 600s BC as well as the 1200s. Defenders of an early setting reply that Pi-Ramesses was abandoned by about 1100 BC and its monuments moved to Tanis, so "Rameses" as a living city name fits the 1200s better (Kitchen, Hoffmeier).
views.J: The Midrash says Israel became idle and forgot covenant ways when Joseph died, and that "a new king" may mean the same king with new policies (Talmud, Sotah 11a). The midwives become models of moral courage, and rabbis identified them with Jochebed and Miriam.
views.X: Matthew's story of Herod killing the boys of Bethlehem echoes Pharaoh's decree, and Jesus, like Moses, is saved from a murderous king (Matthew 2:13–18). Stephen retells the chapter in Acts 7:17–19, and Hebrews 11:23 praises the faith of Moses' parents.

deep.h: Who was the Pharaoh of the oppression?
deep.b:
Exodus never names the king; it uses only the title "Pharaoh," which Egyptians began to use for the king himself around 1450 BC. Two main answers follow two dates for the exodus. Those who take 1 Kings 6:1 literally (480 years from the exodus to Solomon's fourth year, about 966 BC) arrive at about 1446 BC, which makes the oppressor Thutmose I or Thutmose III and the exodus king Amenhotep II. Those who give weight to the city name Rameses (1:11) date the oppression to Seti I and Ramesses II, the great builder of Pi-Ramesses, about 1290–1213 BC, with the exodus in the 1260s or 1250s.

Neither view has a direct Egyptian confirmation. The Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC) shows that a people called Israel was in Canaan by then. Critical scholars think the biblical writers did not have a particular king in mind: "Pharaoh" is the type of the oppressor-king, and the name Rameses was simply the best-known royal city of the past. See the chapter 12 page for the full dating debate.

deep.title: A speculation: why is the king nameless?
deep.b: The narrator names two humble midwives and leaves the most powerful man on earth anonymous. This may be deliberate, a literary point already made by Nahum Sarna, J. Cheryl Exum and Terence Fretheim. In Egypt, a king's name was his immortality: inscriptions were carved to preserve it, and erasing a name (as was done to Hatshepsut and Akhenaten) was a way of destroying a person's memory. Exodus may be doing the same to Pharaoh, while giving eternal memory to Shiphrah and Puah. The link with Egyptian name-erasing is my own suggestion; it fits the text but cannot be proven, and the simple explanation (the title was enough for the first readers) is also possible.

echoes: Genesis 1:28; Genesis 15:13–14; Genesis 46:27; Genesis 50:24–26; Acts 7:17–19; Matthew 2:16–18; Hebrews 11:23; Luke 9:31

settings.what: Pharaoh's speech against Israel
settings.by: The new king of Egypt, "who did not know Joseph"
settings.to: His people, the Egyptians
settings.when: When the Israelites have grown many in the land
settings.why: To turn fear into policy. The Israelites are too many and might side with an enemy in war, so Egypt must outsmart them. The speech launches the forced labor. It is the first state program against a people in the Bible.
settings.readers: For Israel, later ruled by Assyria, Babylon and Persia, such words were familiar. A great power fears a small people and plans to keep it down.

settings.what: Pharaoh's order to the midwives, and their answer
settings.by: The king of Egypt, then the midwives
settings.to: Shiphrah and Puah, the Hebrew midwives; then the king
settings.when: When forced labor fails to stop Israel's growth
settings.why: Pharaoh orders the midwives to kill the Hebrew boys at birth in secret. They fear God and refuse. When he calls them in, they say the Hebrew women "are full of life" and give birth before a midwife arrives. Their answer outwits the king. God makes households for them. It is the first act of civil disobedience in the Bible, and the story keeps their names and not Pharaoh's.
settings.readers: For Israel the midwives showed that fear of God can stand up to a king's command. Two women with no power began the rescue that Moses would finish.

settings.what: Pharaoh's decree to drown the boys
settings.to: All his people
settings.when: When the midwives' refusal defeats him
settings.why: To have every newborn Hebrew son thrown into the Nile. The decree sets up Moses' birth: the river of death becomes the place of his rescue.
settings.readers: For Israel the decree explained the last blow, the death of Egypt's firstborn (11:4–8). Matthew tells of Herod's like order at Jesus' birth (Matthew 2:16).

title: Drawn Out of the Water
sum: A Levite couple has a son and hides him for three months. When they can hide him no longer, his mother makes a little papyrus "ark," coats it with tar, and sets it among the reeds of the Nile. Pharaoh's own daughter finds the crying baby, pities him, and, through the quick thinking of his sister, pays his own mother to nurse him. She names him Moses: "From the water I drew him."

Grown up, Moses sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew and kills him. When his own people reject him ("Who put you as a chief and judge over us?"), he flees to Midian, rescues a priest's daughters at a well, marries Zipporah, and names his son Gershom, "a foreigner there." Back in Egypt, the Israelites groan, and God hears, remembers, sees and knows.
readings: Read as history

A Hebrew boy raised at court is plausible: Egyptian palaces had nurseries (the kap) where foreign princes were raised. Moses' name is Egyptian (-mose, "born of," as in Thutmose). Traditional readers accept the story as the start of Moses' life.
Read as legend

The tale of a baby set adrift and raised by royalty is told of Sargon of Akkad, Cyrus and Romulus. Critical scholars read the Moses birth story as a hero legend that answers why a Hebrew leader had an Egyptian name and how he learned the ways of Pharaoh's court.
Read as a women's story

Five women save Moses before he does anything himself: two midwives, his mother, his sister and Pharaoh's daughter. Then seven daughters of Midian and Zipporah enter the story. Feminist scholars, J. Cheryl Exum among them, note that the liberation of Israel begins in women's disobedience.

views.H: Moses was a real Hebrew raised in an Egyptian court. Acts 7:22 says he was trained "in all the wisdom of the Egyptians." His Egyptian name and the details of papyrus, tar and Nile reeds fit the setting.
views.M: Moses' Egyptian name is one of the strongest pieces of evidence for a historical core: a later Israelite inventing a founder would hardly give him an Egyptian name. Several Levite names in the tradition are Egyptian too.
views.C: The birth story follows the Sargon legend and other ancient exposure tales. It may come from a later period when such stories circulated, and the explanation of the name by a Hebrew pun is a popular etymology. Some critics doubt that Moses can be recovered as a historical person.
views.J: The rabbis said Miriam persuaded her parents to have more children despite Pharaoh's decree, and that Pharaoh's daughter, named Bithiah (1 Chronicles 4:18), went down to the river to purify herself from her father's idols. Moses' killing of the Egyptian is defended: the Midrash says he saw by prophecy that no righteous descendant would come from that man.
views.X: Stephen (Acts 7:20–29) and Hebrews (11:23–27) retell the chapter. Hebrews says Moses "would not be known as the son of Pharaoh's daughter," choosing to suffer with God's people. Many church fathers saw the rejected deliverer as a pattern for Jesus, rejected by his own (John 1:11).

deep.b:
A Neo-Assyrian text (700s BC) has Sargon of Akkad, who ruled about 2300 BC, tell his own birth story: his mother, a priestess, "set me in a basket of rushes, sealed my lid with bitumen, and cast me into the river." A water-drawer raised him, and the goddess Ishtar loved him until he became king. The parallels to Exodus 2 are clear: secret birth, a reed vessel sealed with pitch, a river, rescue by a stranger, and future greatness.

Scholars draw different conclusions. Critical scholars such as Donald Redford and Brian Lewis treat the Moses story as a version of a widespread hero legend. Others note real differences: Moses is not abandoned but carefully placed and watched; his rescuer is a royal woman; he is nursed by his own mother; and he does not rise to be king but chooses his enslaved people. Traditional readers say that a common motif does not make an event unhistorical, since infants really were abandoned in the ancient world.

echoes: Genesis 6:14; Genesis 24:11–20; Genesis 29:1–12; Acts 7:20–29; Hebrews 11:23–27; Matthew 2:13–15

settings.what: The Hebrew's challenge to Moses
settings.to: The Hebrew who is beating his neighbor; then Moses
settings.when: The day after Moses kills an Egyptian
settings.why: Moses asks the man in the wrong why he strikes his neighbor. The man answers, "Who put you as a chief and a judge over us?" and asks whether Moses means to kill him too. Moses realizes the killing is known and runs to Midian. The first time Moses acts as judge, his own people reject him.
settings.readers: For Israel the question returned every time the people turned against Moses in the wilderness. Stephen quotes it as the pattern of Israel rejecting the one God sent (Acts 7:27, 35).

title: The Bush That Did Not Burn
sum: Moses, now a shepherd for his father-in-law Jethro, leads the flock to Horeb, the mountain of God. An angel of the LORD appears in a flame inside a thornbush that burns but is not eaten up. God calls "Moses! Moses!", tells him to take off his sandals, and says he has seen Israel's misery and has come down to rescue them. Moses is to go to Pharaoh.

Moses raises objections. To "Who am I?" God answers, "I will be with you." To "What is his name?" God answers with the mysterious Ehyeh asher ehyeh, "I will be who I will be," and gives the name YHWH, "the LORD," his name forever. Moses is to gather the elders, ask Pharaoh for a three-day journey to worship, and expect a hard refusal. When Israel leaves, they will not go empty-handed.
readings: Read as revelation
A real encounter in which God disclosed his personal name and his plan. Jews and Christians alike treat 3:14 as one of the most important sentences in Scripture about who God is.
Read as a call story

Form critics such as Norman Habel identified a pattern in prophetic call stories: an encounter with God, a commission, an objection, reassurance, and a sign. The same pattern appears for Gideon (Judges 6), Isaiah (6) and Jeremiah (1). Moses' call is the model.
Read philosophically

The Septuagint's "I am the one who is" led Philo, the church fathers, and medieval thinkers such as Maimonides and Thomas Aquinas to see here a statement about God as pure Being. Many modern scholars say the Hebrew is more about presence and action than metaphysics.

views.H: Moses had a real experience of God at a particular mountain, Horeb (Sinai). The name YHWH was revealed or newly explained to him there, and he went back to Egypt in obedience.
views.M: Many scholars think the worship of YHWH came from the south, from Midian, Edom or Seir, where Egyptian texts mention a "land of the Shasu of YHW." Moses, married into a Midianite priest's family, may have learned the name there: the "Midianite-Kenite hypothesis."
views.C: The chapter combines two sources: one (E) that uses "God" until the name is revealed here, and one (J) that uses YHWH from Genesis 2 on. The name's revelation in 3:14–15 is E's account; 6:2–8 is P's. The explanation of the name is a theological wordplay, not its original meaning.
views.J: The Midrash asks why a lowly thornbush: to show that God shares Israel's suffering, "I am at his side in hard times" (Psalm 91:15). Rashi reads 3:14 as "I will be with them in this trouble as I will be in later troubles." Maimonides saw the phrase as describing God's necessary existence.
views.X: Jesus' "Before Abraham came to be, I am" (John 8:58) and his "I am" sayings echo the Greek of 3:14. Jesus also cites the bush to prove the resurrection: God is "the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob," not of the dead but of the living (Mark 12:26–27). Church fathers saw the unburnt bush as a picture of the incarnation or of Mary.

deep.h: What does "I will be who I will be" mean?
deep.b:
The Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh uses the verb hayah, "to be, become, happen," in a form that usually points to the future or to ongoing action. Main readings:

(1) Presence: "I will be there, as I will be there" (Martin Buber, Rashi). God answers "Who am I?" with "I will be with you" (3:12), and the name continues that promise. (2) Being: "I am who I am" (KJV) or "I am the one who is" (Septuagint), a statement of God's self-existence, beloved by Philo, Augustine, Aquinas and Maimonides. (3) A refusal: "I am who I am, and that is all you need to know," a deliberate reply that will not let the name be used as magic (some modern scholars). (4) Cause: William F. Albright and Frank Cross read YHWH as a causative, "he who causes to be," perhaps from a longer formula about creation.

The name YHWH itself seems to be explained as "he will be," the third-person form of ehyeh. This translation uses "I will be," which keeps the verb's openness to the future, and "I Will Be" as the short form in 3:14b.

Jews do not pronounce the four letters YHWH. In reading they say Adonai, "my Lord," and in conversation HaShem, "the Name." The pronunciation "Yahweh" is a scholarly reconstruction based on Greek transcriptions by Clement of Alexandria and Theodoret. "Jehovah" mixes the consonants of YHWH with the vowels of Adonai, and was popularized in the 1500s.
deep.title: Saying the Name

echoes: Genesis 15:13–14; Genesis 22:11; Genesis 50:24; Isaiah 6:1–8; Jeremiah 1:4–10; Mark 12:26; John 8:58; Acts 7:30–34

settings.what: God's call and name at the burning bush
settings.to: Moses, keeping Jethro's flock at Horeb, the mountain of God
settings.when: When he turns aside to look at the bush that does not burn up
settings.why: To send Moses to Pharaoh to bring Israel out. God says he has seen, heard and come down. He answers "Who am I?" with "I will be with you." He gives his name: "I will be who I will be," and the LORD (YHWH), the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He also lays out the plan. The elders will listen, Pharaoh will refuse, God will strike Egypt with wonders, and Israel will leave with Egypt's silver and gold.
settings.readers: For Israel the scene told who their God is: one who sees slaves and keeps his promises to their fathers. His name was the pledge that he would be present with them.
views: Traditional readers hold that the name was known before, and that here its meaning is revealed.
Many critical scholars read 3:1–4:17 and 6:2–8 as two versions of Moses' call from different sources. In the Elohist (E) and Priestly (P) sources the name YHWH is first made known to Moses.

Many Jewish readers hear "I will be who I will be" as God's faithful presence. The Septuagint ("I am the one who is") and much Christian theology read it as pure being. Others hear a refusal to be controlled by a name.

title: Signs, Excuses, and a Night Attack
sum: Moses fears the people will not believe him, so God gives him three signs: a staff that becomes a snake, a hand that turns diseased and is healed, and Nile water that becomes blood. Moses pleads that he is "heavy of mouth." God answers that he made human mouths, and when Moses still begs him to send someone else, God, angry, gives him Aaron as a spokesman.

Moses takes his family back toward Egypt, staff in hand. God warns that he will make Pharaoh's heart stubborn and gives the message: "Israel is my son, my firstborn... if you refuse, I will kill your firstborn." On the road, in a strange scene, the LORD tries to kill Moses until Zipporah circumcises their son. Aaron meets Moses at the mountain, and the elders of Israel believe and worship.
readings: Read as history

God equipped a reluctant leader with signs and a partner. The episode at the lodging place is real but mysterious, a reminder that the covenant sign of circumcision could not be ignored even by Moses.
Read as a portrait of a reluctant prophet

Moses makes five objections, more than any other called figure. The Bible's greatest prophet is also its most reluctant one, and God's anger here does not cancel the call. Readers find comfort that God works through limited, frightened people.
Read as ancient religion

Critical scholars see in 4:24–26 a very old fragment about a dangerous divine encounter and a blood rite that protects, a cousin of the Passover blood on the doorposts. Zipporah's words may preserve an ancient formula whose meaning was lost even to the editors.

views.H: Moses received real signs, and Aaron really became his spokesman. The night attack shows God's seriousness about the covenant sign. Traditional chronologies place this about 1446 or 1260 BC.
views.M: Aaron's place beside Moses may reflect the joining of two priestly groups, the Aaronides and the Levites, each with its own founder figure. Zipporah, a Midianite, preserves the memory of Midian's role in Israel's early worship.
views.C: The chapter combines sources. 4:1–17 (often J and E) gives Moses a partner; 6:10–7:7 (P) tells the same story again. The bridegroom of blood (4:24–26) is among the oldest fragments in the Torah, perhaps explaining infant circumcision.
views.J: Targum Onkelos and the Septuagint say an angel attacked Moses; the Talmud (Nedarim 31b–32a) says Moses delayed circumcising his son and was punished for it. The Midrash teaches that Moses' "heavy" speech came from a burning coal he put to his mouth as a child in Pharaoh's palace.
views.X: Christians read "Israel is my son, my firstborn" alongside Hosea 11:1 and Matthew 2:15, "Out of Egypt I called my son," applied to Jesus. Paul quotes 4:21's theme of hardening in Romans 9. Some fathers saw the staff that became a snake as a sign of Christ lifted up (Numbers 21:9; John 3:14).

deep.b:
Three verses, many unanswered questions. Whom did the LORD try to kill: Moses or his son? Whose "feet" (perhaps a euphemism) did Zipporah touch with the foreskin? Who is the "bridegroom of blood"?

Traditional answers: Moses had neglected to circumcise his son, and Zipporah saved him by doing it (Talmud, Nedarim 31b). The Septuagint says an angel attacked and Zipporah said, "The blood of my child's circumcision has stopped." Critical readings: the scene preserves an archaic story of a demon or deity of the night whose attack is turned away by blood, later applied to the LORD. William Propp argued that it concerns Moses' blood guilt for killing the Egyptian, removed by the blood of circumcision. Literary readers note the links with Passover (blood, firstborn sons, a night threat) and with Jacob's night struggle (Genesis 32), each a dangerous meeting with God before a great return.

echoes: Genesis 17:9–14; Genesis 32:22–32; Numbers 12:3; Numbers 21:8–9; Hosea 11:1; Matthew 2:15; Matthew 2:20; Romans 9:17–18

settings.what: The signs and Moses' objections
settings.to: Moses, still at the bush
settings.when: Continuing the call
settings.why: Moses fears no one will believe him, then pleads that he is no speaker, then begs God to send someone else. God gives three signs and reminds him who makes mouths. Angry, God gives him Aaron as his spokesman. The prophet is chosen in his weakness, not for his skill.
settings.readers: For Israel this was the pattern of a true prophet, who does not want the task. Jeremiah later resisted his call in the same way (Jeremiah 1:6).

settings.what: The message about Israel, God's firstborn
settings.to: Moses, who is to say it to Pharaoh
settings.when: On the road back to Egypt
settings.why: To give the heart of the coming conflict: "Israel is my son, my firstborn." If Pharaoh will not let God's son go to serve him, God will kill Pharaoh's firstborn. The words explain the last blow in advance.
settings.readers: For Israel this was its standing as God's son. The title was later given to the king (Psalm 2:7), and Matthew applies it to Jesus (Matthew 2:15, quoting Hosea 11:1).

settings.what: Zipporah's words at the night attack
settings.to: The LORD's attacker, or Moses, or her son; the text does not say clearly
settings.when: At a stopping place on the road to Egypt, when the LORD seeks to kill Moses or his son
settings.why: She cuts off her son's foreskin with a flint, touches it to "his feet," and speaks of a bridegroom of blood. The attack stops. The strange scene shows that the man sent to free God's firstborn must first keep the covenant sign in his own family (Genesis 17:14).
settings.readers: For Israel the scene pointed ahead to the blood on the doorposts that would turn the destroyer away (12:23). It also taught that the covenant sign was a matter of life and death.
views: Most readers think the LORD sought to kill Moses for not circumcising his son.
Some think Moses' firstborn son was in danger, matching 4:22–23.
Some critical scholars (Propp) see an ancient tradition about circumcision and blood whose meaning was already unclear.

title: Bricks Without Straw
sum: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let Israel go into the wilderness to hold a feast. Pharaoh answers, "Who is the LORD, that I should heed his voice? I do not know the LORD." Instead of relief, he orders the Israelites to gather their own straw while making the same number of bricks, calling them lazy.

The Israelite foremen are beaten for missed quotas and complain to Pharaoh, then to Moses and Aaron: "You have made us reek in Pharaoh's eyes." Moses turns to God with his own complaint: "Why have you brought harm on this people? Why ever did you send me?" The first round has made things worse.
readings: Read as history

Egyptian documents describe brick quotas, straw in bricks, and records of absent workers. The Louvre Leather Roll from the reign of Ramesses II records a shortfall in brick production; a letter in Papyrus Anastasi IV complains that there are no men to make bricks and no straw. Traditional readers find the chapter's setting realistic.
Read as a story about power

Pharaoh's "I do not know the LORD" sets up the question of the following chapters: will he come to know? He treats religious desire as idleness, divides foremen from workers, and turns the oppressed against their leaders, techniques readers have recognized in many tyrannies.
Read as a lament

Moses' prayer at the end begins a tradition of honest complaint to God (Psalms of lament, Jeremiah, Job). God does not rebuke him. The chapter teaches that liberation can get harder before it gets easier.

views.H: A real negotiation that went badly. The details of brickmaking with and without straw, quotas and foremen fit New Kingdom Egypt.
views.M: A memory of forced labor in Egyptian building projects, which Egyptian records show used Asiatic workers. The "feast in the wilderness" may preserve an early pilgrimage festival to a southern mountain of YHWH.
views.C: The first confrontation is shaped to set up the plague narrative. Brickmaking details were common knowledge throughout the ancient Near East, and do not prove an early date. The repeated "three-day journey" may reflect an older version in which Israel escaped during a festival.
views.J: The Midrash says the tribe of Levi was exempt from slavery because they studied Torah, and that the Israelite foremen let themselves be beaten rather than punish their people, so they were later chosen as the seventy elders (Rashi on Numbers 11:16). Moses' complaint is defended as a bold act of love for Israel.
views.X: Christian writers took Pharaoh's "Who is the LORD?" as the voice of unbelief and pride. Bricks without straw became a proverb for impossible demands. Hebrews 11:25 says Moses chose to suffer with God's people rather than enjoy sin's pleasures.

settings.what: The first demand and Pharaoh's answer
settings.to: Pharaoh, then Moses and Aaron
settings.when: Their first audience with Pharaoh
settings.why: Moses and Aaron bring the LORD's word, "Let my people go," so that they may hold a feast to him in the wilderness. Pharaoh answers that he does not know the LORD and will not let Israel go.
settings.readers: For Israel the rest of the book answered Pharaoh's question, "Who is this LORD?" The exodus was a contest over who is God, and whom Israel will serve.

settings.what: Pharaoh's order of bricks without straw
settings.by: Pharaoh, through his slave drivers and the Israelite officers
settings.to: The slave drivers and officers, and through them every Israelite laborer
settings.when: The same day as the first demand
settings.why: To crush hope by making the work harder: gather your own straw and still make the same number of bricks. When the Israelite officers protest, Pharaoh calls them lazy. The decree shows how oppressors answer a call for freedom.
settings.readers: For Israel, which later knew forced labor under its own kings (1 Kings 12:4) and under foreign empires, the pattern was familiar.

settings.what: The officers' curse and Moses' complaint
settings.to: Moses and Aaron; then the LORD
settings.when: As the officers come out from Pharaoh
settings.why: The officers call on the LORD to judge Moses and Aaron for making them reek in Pharaoh's eyes. Moses turns to God: "Why have you brought harm on this people? Why ever did you send me?"
settings.readers: For Israel the Bible kept the prophet's bitter question as a pattern for its own laments to God (Psalm 44).

title: I Am the LORD
sum: God answers Moses' complaint with a solemn speech: "I am the LORD." He appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as God Almighty (El Shaddai), "but my name, the LORD, I did not make known to them." He has heard Israel's groaning and remembered his covenant. Seven promises follow: I will lead you out, snatch you out, redeem you, take you as my people, be your God, bring you into the land, and give it to you.

Israel is too crushed in spirit to listen. Moses protests again that he has "uncircumcised lips." The story pauses for a genealogy of Reuben, Simeon and Levi, which traces Moses and Aaron to Levi, Kohath and Amram, names their wives and sons, and ends with Phinehas, the future priest.
readings: Read as a second call
Many readers see 6:2–7:7 as a second commissioning after the failure of chapter 5, renewing God's promise in stronger terms. The genealogy confirms the leaders' credentials before the plagues begin.
Read as a second source

Source critics see the Priestly (P) account of Moses' call, parallel to J/E in chapter 3. In P, the name YHWH was first revealed to Moses, which explains why P uses only "God" and "God Almighty" in Genesis.
Read in the Seder
The Jerusalem Talmud links the four cups of Passover wine to the verbs of 6:6–7, and a fifth cup, Elijah's cup, is often linked to 6:8. The verses are a liturgical creed of redemption.

views.H: God did not reveal a new name but its full meaning. The patriarchs knew the word YHWH (Genesis 15:7; 28:13) but had not experienced the power behind it, which the exodus would show. This is the view of Rashi, Ramban, and many traditional Christian scholars.
views.M: The verse preserves a real memory that YHWH worship came to Israel with Moses' group, while other ancestors worshiped El, the high god of Canaan, and his titles such as El Shaddai. The two traditions were merged when the groups joined.
views.C: This is the key text for source criticism of the Pentateuch since Jean Astruc (1753). In the Priestly source, the name was unknown before Moses; in J, people called on the name of the LORD from Genesis 4:26. The contradiction shows that separate sources were combined.
views.J: Rashi: "I was not known to them by my attribute of faithfulness," since they received promises but did not see them fulfilled. The four verbs of redemption gave the Seder its four cups. Rashi explains why the genealogy names Reuben, Simeon and Levi: Jacob had rebuked these three (Genesis 49:3–7), so the Torah lists them here to show they were still honored.
views.X: Christians read the progressive revelation of God's name as reaching its fullness in Jesus: "I have let them know your name" (John 17:26). The genealogy ending with Phinehas and Aaron is read as preparing for the priesthood that Hebrews contrasts with Christ's.

deep.h: Did the patriarchs know the name YHWH? (6:3)
deep.b:
Genesis uses YHWH over 150 times, and the patriarchs themselves use it (Genesis 15:2; 28:16). Yet here God says, "my name, the LORD, I did not make known to them." How can both be true?

(1) The name's meaning, not its sound: "to know a name" means to experience what the name stands for. The patriarchs knew God as the promiser, El Shaddai; Israel will know him as the one who keeps his word (Rashi, Ramban, Calvin). (2) A question: some read the second clause as a question, "by my name the LORD did I not make myself known?" (a minority view). (3) Sources: the Priestly writer held that the name was unknown before Moses, and avoided it in his Genesis material; the J writer used it throughout. When the sources were combined, the tension remained. This observation began modern source criticism.

(4) Historical: the patriarchal religion was the worship of El, the chief god of Canaan, under titles like El Shaddai, El Elyon and El Olam; YHWH worship arrived with the exodus group. Frank Cross developed this view in Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic.

echoes: Genesis 4:26; Genesis 15:7; Genesis 17:1; Genesis 28:13; Genesis 35:11; Numbers 26:57–61; 1 Chronicles 6:1–3; Ezekiel 20:5–6

settings.what: The promise "I am the LORD"
settings.to: Moses, to tell the Israelites
settings.when: In answer to Moses' complaint
settings.why: To restate the covenant. God appeared to the fathers as God Almighty, but by his name, the LORD, he did not make himself known to them. He has heard the groaning and remembered his covenant. Seven promises follow. I will bring you out, rescue you, redeem you, take you as my people, and be your God. I will bring you into the land and give it to you.
settings.readers: For Israel the promises became part of its worship: at the Passover Seder four cups of wine are tied to four of these verbs. For exiles in Babylon, a promise of redemption from slavery and return to the land spoke again.
views: The name's meaning, not the name
Traditional readers (Rashi, Ramban) hold that the fathers knew the name but had not seen the faithfulness it stands for.
Many critical scholars take 6:3 at its word, as the Priestly source's claim that the name was first given to Moses. It is a key text for the source theory.

settings.what: Moses as God to Pharaoh
settings.to: Moses, who has objected that his lips are uncircumcised
settings.when: In Egypt, before the first sign
settings.why: To make Moses like God to Pharaoh, with Aaron as his prophet. God warns that he will make Pharaoh's heart hard and multiply his signs. So Egypt will know that he is the LORD when he brings Israel out. The words prepare Moses for a long struggle and give its purpose.
settings.readers: For Israel the purpose was striking: even its oppressors were to come to know God.
views: Some readers stress that God hardens Pharaoh's heart as his own act of judgment and power (compare Romans 9:17–18).
Others note that Pharaoh first hardens his own heart, and that God confirms the choice he has made.

title: A Staff That Swallowed Staffs
sum: God makes Moses "as God" to Pharaoh, with Aaron as his prophet, and warns that he will make Pharaoh's heart hard and multiply his signs. Moses is eighty and Aaron eighty-three. Before Pharaoh, Aaron's staff becomes a serpent; the Egyptian magicians do the same with their spells, but Aaron's staff swallows theirs. Pharaoh's heart stays stubborn.

The first blow follows. Meeting Pharaoh by the Nile in the morning, Moses strikes the water, and the river turns to blood. The fish die, the river stinks, and the Egyptians cannot drink. The magicians imitate it, and Pharaoh walks home unmoved. For seven days Egypt digs for water along the river.
readings: Read as miracle
God turned the Nile to real blood, a judgment on the river that Egypt worshiped and that had swallowed Israel's sons (1:22). The magicians' imitation shows that evil powers can copy but not undo.
Read as a natural disaster

Greta Hort and others propose that an unusually high flood brought red earth and toxic algae (perhaps a "red tide" of flagellates) that colored the river, killed fish and drove frogs out, starting a chain of plagues.
Read as polemic

The contest of staffs and the attack on the Nile are a challenge to Egypt's gods and to Pharaoh's claim to keep cosmic order. The serpent, a symbol of royal power on Pharaoh's crown (the uraeus), is swallowed.

views.H: The plagues were real events, either pure miracles or natural events heightened and timed by God. Egyptian details (magicians, the Nile, the morning visit) show the author knew Egypt.
views.M: Natural disasters, remembered and enlarged, may lie behind the plague stories, perhaps among an Egyptian-dwelling group whose escape coincided with disaster.
views.C: The plagues are a literary construction. Psalms 78 and 105 list seven or eight plagues in different orders, which suggests the ten-plague cycle grew over time. J's plagues are acts of God announced by Moses; P's are contests in which Aaron's staff performs wonders; they have been woven together.
views.J: The Midrash says each plague lasted a month, with three weeks of warning and one of suffering, and that the blood plague struck first because Egypt worshiped the Nile. Aaron, not Moses, struck the water, because the river had once protected the baby Moses (Rashi on 7:19).
views.X: Revelation's trumpets and bowls (Revelation 8; 16) reuse the plagues of Egypt, turning water to blood and sending darkness, sores, hail and frogs. 2 Timothy 3:8 names the magicians Jannes and Jambres.

deep.h: The plagues: natural causes or miracle?
deep.b:
Greta Hort's two articles (1957–58) are the classic natural explanation: a heavy Nile flood in late summer carries red soil and algae (plague 1); frogs leave the poisoned river and die (2); mosquitoes and flies breed (3–4); anthrax from the frog carcasses kills cattle (5) and causes skin sores (6); a spring hailstorm (7), east winds bringing locusts (8) and a khamsin dust storm (9) follow. The tenth plague has no natural explanation in her scheme, though others have proposed poisoned grain stores eaten first by firstborn sons.

Siro Trevisanato tied the plagues to the Thera (Santorini) eruption, but that eruption is usually dated about 1600 BC, a strong objection. For the natural view: the sequence fits Egypt's seasons and ecology; the text itself says God used wind (10:13, 19; 14:21). Against: the plagues come and go at Moses' word, Goshen is spared, and the text presents them as unprecedented. Many believers take a middle way: God worked through nature with miraculous timing and intensity. Critical scholars think the search for natural causes misreads a literary and theological composition.

deep.title: A speculation: the first blow and the last
deep.b: The first plague turns the Nile, which received Israel's drowned sons (1:22), into blood, and the last takes Egypt's firstborn sons. That the blood plague answers the decree against the infants is not new: Wisdom of Solomon 11:6–7 says that in place of the river's never-failing spring Egypt was given "foul, gory blood as a rebuke for the order to kill the babies," and the Midrash ties the first plague to 1:22. What I add is the frame: the cycle may be built so that its first and last blows both answer the crime against Israel's sons, the river first, Pharaoh's own house last. That framing is my inference from the structure, not a claim the book makes.

title: The Finger of God
sum: Three more blows fall. Frogs swarm up from the Nile into houses, beds and ovens; the magicians copy them, but Pharaoh begs Moses to pray, and when the frogs die in stinking heaps, he goes back on his word. Next, Aaron strikes the dust, and it becomes gnats on people and animals. The magicians fail and admit, "It is the finger of God."

The fourth blow, swarms, comes with a new feature: God sets Goshen apart, "so that you will know that I am the LORD, here in the middle of the land." Pharaoh offers to let Israel sacrifice in Egypt, then just outside it; Moses refuses any compromise. When the swarms leave, Pharaoh once again makes his heart heavy.
readings: Read as a contest

The magicians match the first two plagues, fail at the third, and disappear after the sixth. Egypt's experts are defeated step by step, and Pharaoh, who once said he did not know the LORD, is learning.
Read as structure

From here the plagues come in three sets of three. Each set opens with a morning warning by the river, continues with a warning in the palace, and ends with a plague that comes without warning. The distinction between Egypt and Israel begins in the second set.
Read as negotiation
Pharaoh's offers shrink and stretch: "sacrifice in the land," "not too far," later "men only" and "no flocks." Moses' refusals show that true worship cannot be squeezed into Egypt's terms.

views.H: Real plagues, increasingly serious, with Goshen spared from the fourth on. The details of Egyptian religion (sacred animals, the frog goddess Heqet) suggest an author who knew Egypt.
views.M: A memory of natural disasters in the eastern Delta, interpreted by a small group of escapees as the acts of their God.
views.C: The frog and gnat plagues contain P's typical features (Aaron's staff, the magicians); the swarm plague is J. Their combination produced the present pattern. The concern with sacrifices that would offend Egyptians may reflect later Jewish life in Egypt (for example, the Jewish temple at Elephantine, destroyed by Egyptians in 410 BC).
views.J: The Midrash says one frog came up and multiplied as it was struck. The "finger of God" taught the Haggadah to count fifty plagues at the sea. The rabbis noted that frogs went even into hot ovens, and Daniel's friends learned from them to enter the furnace for God's sake (Talmud, Pesachim 53b).
views.X: Jesus says he drives out demons "by God's finger" (Luke 11:20), claiming the authority that defeated Egypt's magicians. Revelation 16:13 sees "evil spirits that looked like frogs" coming out of the dragon's mouth. Christian writers often used Pharaoh's broken promises as a warning against bargains with God.

settings.what: The magicians' admission
settings.to: Pharaoh
settings.when: When they cannot copy the gnats
settings.why: To admit defeat: "It is the finger of God." Egypt's own experts are the first Egyptians to name God's hand in the blows. Pharaoh's heart stays hard all the same.
settings.readers: For Israel the wise men of the empire had to confess what their king would not. Jesus uses the phrase of his own power over demons (Luke 11:20).

title: Hail Like Never Before
sum: The fifth blow kills Egypt's livestock in the field, but not one Israelite animal dies; Pharaoh checks and still refuses. The sixth comes without warning: Moses throws kiln soot into the air, and it becomes festering sores on people and animals. The magicians cannot even stand before Moses. For the first time the narrator says, "The LORD made Pharaoh's heart stubborn."

Before the seventh blow God explains his purpose: he could have wiped Egypt out, but has kept Pharaoh standing "to let you see my strength, and so that my name will be told in all the earth." A warning is given, and some Egyptian officials who fear the LORD bring their animals inside. Thunder, hail and fire strike everything in the fields except Goshen. Pharaoh confesses, "I have sinned," but when the storm stops, he sins again.
readings: Read as judgment and mercy
The hail plague is the first to offer Egyptians a way of escape, and some take it. Judgment and warning go together, and the narrator separates those who fear God's word from those who ignore it.
Read as theology of hardening

This chapter is the turning point: before it, Pharaoh hardens himself or his heart simply "is" hard; at the sixth plague, for the first time, God hardens it (9:12). Even so, Pharaoh hardens himself once more after the hail (9:34). Paul quotes 9:16 in Romans 9:17, making it a central text for debates about divine choice and human freedom.
Read as history and ecology
Farming details (flax and barley struck, wheat and spelt spared) fit Egypt in about February. Those who read the plagues naturally see a severe late-winter storm following disease among livestock.

views.H: Real events of judgment, distinguished by God's protection of Israel. The precise agricultural details point to an author familiar with Egypt.
views.M: Livestock disease and destructive storms are known in Egypt; a small escaping group may have remembered such events and read them as signs. The theology of hardening came later.
views.C: The livestock plague (J) and the sores (P) come from different sources, which explains why livestock killed in 9:6 are hit again in 9:19–25. The speech of 9:14–16 states the theme of the whole cycle: the LORD's name made known in all the earth.
views.J: Rashi and Maimonides stress that Pharaoh hardened himself during the first five plagues, so the later hardenings are punishment; Sforno instead says God strengthened Pharaoh so that his choice would stay free. The God-fearing officials in 9:20 are praised; one tradition identifies Job among them. The Midrash notes that fire and water, enemies by nature, made peace in the hail to do God's will.
views.X: Paul's use of 9:16 (Romans 9:17) shaped Augustine's and Calvin's doctrine of election and reprobation. Arminians, from Jacobus Arminius's own analysis of Romans 9 to John Wesley, read it as conditional: God hardens those who first resist him. Others, such as Brian Abasciano, read Paul as speaking of the election of a people in history; John Chrysostom, for the Orthodox, stressed Pharaoh's free choice. Both the individual and the corporate readings are held today. Revelation 16:21 echoes the giant hail.

deep.b:
The heart is mentioned about twenty times in chapters 4–14. Three patterns appear: God hardens (4:21; 7:3; 9:12; 10:1, 20, 27; 11:10; 14:4, 8, 17); Pharaoh hardens his own heart (8:15, 32; 9:34); and the heart simply "was" hard (7:13, 14, 22; 8:19; 9:7, 35). God's hardening is foretold first but is narrated as an act only from the sixth plague on.

Jewish tradition (Exodus Rabbah, Rashi, Maimonides) reads this as moral cause and effect: Pharaoh's free choices became a fixed character, and God confirmed the choice as punishment, removing the gate of repentance. Origen and many Greek fathers said God's goodness itself hardens a resisting heart, as sun hardens mud. Augustine and Calvin stressed God's sovereign decree, while holding Pharaoh responsible. Sforno (on 7:3), followed by many modern scholars, read "make strong" (chazaq) as God strengthening Pharaoh's resolve so that he acted freely, not merely forced by terror; Ramban gives both this and the penalty view. Arminian writers (Arminius, Wesley) take the hardening as God's response to Pharaoh's prior resistance. Literary critics see the theme serving the story's purpose: to show that the LORD alone controls events, even the will of Egypt's god-king.

echoes: Romans 9:14–18; Psalm 78:47–50; Psalm 105:32–33; Joshua 2:10; 1 Samuel 6:6; Revelation 16:2; Revelation 16:21

settings.what: The purpose of the blows
settings.to: Pharaoh and his servants
settings.when: After the sores, before the hail
settings.why: To explain why the blows go on. God could have wiped Egypt out, but has kept Pharaoh standing to show his strength and to have his name told in all the earth. The warning also offers mercy: bring people and animals in from the field. Some of Pharaoh's servants fear the word and obey (9:20).
settings.readers: For Israel this was the meaning of the whole plague cycle: God's name made known among the nations. Paul quotes 9:16 in Romans 9:17.

traditions.q: When God hardens Pharaoh (9:12, 16), does he choose some people for salvation and pass over others?
views: Yes. Following Paul's use of 9:16 in Romans 9:17, the Westminster Confession teaches that God has chosen some to eternal life and passed over others, leaving them to the just result of their sin (3.3, 3.7). Pharaoh is still fully responsible for his own hardness (Calvin, Institutes 3.21–24).

God's choosing is the cause of salvation only; no one is chosen for damnation, and those who are lost have rejected grace (Formula of Concord, article 11). Lutherans hold both truths without explaining how they fit.

God predestines no one to hell; that requires a free turning from God held to the end (Catechism 1037). Catholics may explain grace and freedom in more than one way: Thomists stress God's grace that moves the will, Molinists God's knowledge of free choices, and in 1607 Pope Paul V allowed both schools.

God foreknows but does not cause anyone's ruin. John Chrysostom read Pharaoh's hardening as the result of Pharaoh's own free choices, and the Orthodox teach synergy, God's grace and human freedom working together.

Wesley preached that Christ died for all and that God's grace is free to all, attacking the idea of a decree passing people by ("Free Grace," 1739). God hardened Pharaoh only after Pharaoh had hardened himself.

Baptists are divided. Calvinistic Baptists follow the 1689 Confession, which matches Westminster; many others hold that God's choice is consistent with human free will, which the Baptist Faith and Message (2000) affirms without settling the question.

title: Locusts and Darkness
sum: God tells Moses he has made Pharaoh's heart heavy so that Israel can tell its children and grandchildren what he did in Egypt. Moses warns of locusts. Pharaoh's officials beg him to give in: "Have you still not grasped that Egypt is lost?" Pharaoh offers to let the men go, but not the children, and drives Moses out. An east wind brings locusts that devour everything green the hail had left.

Pharaoh confesses again, a west wind sweeps the locusts into the Sea of Reeds, and his heart is made stubborn again. Then, without warning, three days of thick darkness fall on Egypt, while Israel has light in its homes. Pharaoh offers to let everyone go but the animals; Moses insists, "Not one hoof will stay behind." Pharaoh threatens death if Moses sees his face again, and Moses agrees.
readings: Read as the end of negotiation
Pharaoh's offers grow but never reach full release; Moses' refusals grow firmer. The chapter ends with a final break: neither will see the other again. The negotiation stage is over.
Read as anti-creation

The locusts cover "the eye of the land" and darkness covers Egypt. Creation's first gift, light (Genesis 1:3), is taken from Egypt but kept for Israel. Terence Fretheim reads the plagues as creation itself turning against the oppressor.
Read as a lesson for children
The chapter begins with a command to tell the next generation. The plagues are not only history but a teaching tool, which is how they are used in the Passover Haggadah to this day.

views.H: Real locust swarms and supernatural darkness. Locusts arriving on an east wind and leaving on a west wind fit the region. The darkness lasting three days but sparing Israel's homes is miraculous.
views.M: Locust swarms and the khamsin dust storms of Egypt's spring are real hazards and may stand behind the memory.
views.C: The locust plague is J's longest and most dramatic, with a story about Pharaoh's officials; the darkness plague is likely E or P. Their combination produces two climactic, contrasting episodes before the final blow.
views.J: Rashi says the darkness had two stages, and that during it the Israelites who did not want to leave died and were buried unseen by the Egyptians. Rashi also explains 10:10 through a star called Evil. The Seder reads 10:2 as a command to tell the story.
views.X: Joel's locust army and Revelation's demonic locusts (Revelation 9:3–11) draw on this chapter. The darkness at noon when Jesus died (Mark 15:33), lasting three hours, has been linked by some Christian readers with Egypt's three days of darkness, followed by the death of the firstborn.

echoes: Joel 1:4; Joel 2:1–11; Psalm 105:28; Psalm 105:34–35; Wisdom of Solomon 17:1–18:4; Mark 15:33; Revelation 9:3–11

settings.what: The reason to tell the story
settings.to: Moses
settings.when: Before the warning of locusts
settings.why: To tell Moses that God has made Pharaoh's heart heavy so that he can put his signs among the Egyptians. The aside names who the story is for: Israel will tell its children and grandchildren how God made sport of Egypt.
settings.readers: For Israel this was a command about the story itself. Parents were to retell the plagues to their children, as the Passover rules also require (12:26–27; 13:14).

title: One More Blow
sum: God tells Moses one last blow is coming, after which Pharaoh will not just let Israel go but drive them out. The people are to ask their Egyptian neighbors for silver and gold, and the Egyptians, who now respect Israel and Moses, will give them freely.

Moses announces the final plague: about midnight the LORD will go through Egypt, and every firstborn will die, from Pharaoh's heir to the son of the slave woman at the hand mill, and the firstborn of animals. There will be a great cry, but not a dog will growl at Israel. Moses leaves Pharaoh in hot anger. A closing summary repeats that Pharaoh would not listen, so God's wonders would be many.
readings: Read as the climax
A short chapter that announces the tenth plague in solemn, poetic terms. Its brevity builds suspense before the night of chapter 12.
Read as an ethical problem

The death of children for the sins of a king is the hardest part of the exodus story. Jewish and Christian readers have answered with measure for measure (1:22), with the many warnings Pharaoh ignored, and with traditions that refuse to rejoice at the enemy's fall.
Read as justice for workers
The gifts of silver and gold are presented as justice: Israel's unpaid wages. The law later requires that a freed slave not be sent away empty-handed (Deuteronomy 15:13–15).

views.H: A real final plague, announced and then carried out at the stated time. The respect shown to Moses explains the gifts of the Egyptians.
views.M: Some memory of a deadly epidemic or disaster may lie behind the tradition, but the identification with firstborn sons belongs to Israel's later theology of the firstborn.
views.C: Chapter 11 seems to interrupt the scene at the end of chapter 10: 11:1–3 is a separate piece, and 11:4–8 completes the last meeting with Pharaoh. 11:9–10 is a Priestly summary of the plague cycle.
views.J: The Haggadah lists the tenth plague as the one God did "by himself, not by an angel." At the Seder, a drop of wine is spilled for each plague to lessen the joy of victory. The Talmud's tradition that God silenced the angels' song when Egyptians drowned (Megillah 10b) is often quoted here.
views.X: The death of the firstborn and the sparing of Israel's sons became a pattern for the death of God's own firstborn Son. Hebrews 11:28 says Moses kept the Passover "by faith," so the destroyer would not touch Israel's firstborn.

settings.what: Instructions before the last blow
settings.to: Moses, to tell the people
settings.when: After the darkness
settings.why: To announce one more blow, after which Pharaoh will drive them out. Every man and woman is to ask their Egyptian neighbors for silver and gold. The request keeps the promise to Abraham that his offspring would come out with great wealth (Genesis 15:14).
settings.readers: For Israel the gold and silver were back wages for the years of slavery, as the rabbis said. The same treasure later built the tabernacle (35:22).

settings.what: The warning of the death of the firstborn
settings.to: Pharaoh and his servants
settings.when: At the last meeting, before Moses leaves in hot anger
settings.why: To announce that about midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh's heir to the son of the slave woman at the mill. Not even a dog will growl at Israel. The blow answers Pharaoh's drowning of Israel's sons (1:22) and the warning of 4:23.
settings.readers: For Israel this was the night on which its whole calendar turned. The difference God made between Egypt and Israel (11:7) is the reason for the Passover.

title: The Night of Passover
sum: Before the last blow, God gives Israel a calendar and a rite. This month will be their first. On the tenth day each household chooses a lamb or kid; on the fourteenth they slaughter it at twilight, put its blood on the doorposts and lintel, and eat it roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, dressed for the road. "I will see the blood and pass over you." A seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread is to be kept forever.

At midnight the LORD strikes every firstborn in Egypt. Pharaoh calls Moses in the night: "Get up, get out... and bless me too." Israel leaves in haste with unrisen dough, Egyptian silver and gold, and a mixed crowd: about 600,000 men on foot from Rameses to Succoth, after 430 years in Egypt. Rules follow: no outsider may eat unless circumcised; one law for native and foreigner.
readings: Read as founding event

The chapter tells how Israel became a people, and how each generation re-enacts its birth. For Jews, Passover is the central festival of memory; the Haggadah says each person must see himself as if he came out of Egypt.
Read as liturgy

Much of the chapter is ritual law, not narrative: the calendar, the lamb, the leaven, the questions of children, who may eat. Scholars note that the story is told through its rite, so that every Passover becomes part of the event.
Read as a type of Christ

Christians read the lamb without defect, the blood that saves, the unbroken bones, and the escape from death as a picture of Jesus' death at Passover: "Our Passover, Christ, has been slaughtered" (1 Corinthians 5:7).

views.H: The first Passover was kept on the night of the exodus, which traditional chronology dates to 1446 BC (1 Kings 6:1) or about 1260 BC. The 600,000 men are either a literal number or a figure using "thousand" for a clan unit.
views.M: Friedman and others think the Levites, a group with Egyptian names, brought the memory of escape and of the Passover rite into Israel. The "mixed crowd" fits a historical core of mixed peoples who joined Israel later.
views.C: Passover was originally a herders' spring rite and Unleavened Bread a farmers' festival, joined in Israel's history (Deuteronomy 16) and linked to the exodus story. The chapter combines P's detailed laws (12:1–20, 43–51) with J's story (12:21–39). No record of a mass exodus exists.
views.J: Passover is kept for eight days outside Israel, seven within, beginning with the Seder. The Mishnah (Pesachim 10) outlines the meal: four cups, the four questions, the story told from "disgrace" to "praise," and Rabban Gamaliel's three essentials: pesach, matzah, maror. Samaritans still sacrifice lambs on Mount Gerizim.
views.X: The Last Supper was set at Passover, and Jesus died at the festival. The Synoptic Gospels present the Supper as a Passover meal; John puts the crucifixion when the lambs were slaughtered. The Christian Easter (Greek Pascha) grew from Passover, and its date was fixed at the Council of Nicaea (AD 325).

deep.h: When was the exodus? 1446 or the 1260s BC
deep.b:
The early date (about 1446 BC) takes 1 Kings 6:1 literally: Solomon began the Temple in his fourth year (about 966 BC), "in the 480th year" after the exodus. Judges 11:26 (Jephthah's 300 years) is cited in support. Defenders (John Bimson, Bryant Wood, Eugene Merrill) date the destruction of Jericho and other cities to about 1400 BC and identify the Habiru of the Amarna letters (1350s BC) with invading Israelites. They take "Rameses" in 1:11 and 12:37 as an updated name. Some also cite the Berlin pedestal relief 21687, read by Manfred Görg, Peter van der Veen and Christoffer Theis as a possible mention of "Israel" before Merneptah; the reading is disputed.

The late date (about 1260s BC) gives weight to the city Rameses (Pi-Ramesses, built by Ramesses II from about 1270 BC), to the lack of settled kingdoms in Edom and Moab before the 1200s (an argument from Nelson Glueck's surveys that is weaker than it once seemed, since settled Edom is now dated mainly later), and to the appearance of hundreds of new hill-country villages in Canaan after 1200 BC. The Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC) names "Israel" as a people in Canaan. Kenneth Kitchen and James Hoffmeier favor this date and read the 480 years as twelve generations of forty years, real generations being closer to twenty-five years.

David Rohl proposed moving Egyptian chronology itself, so the exodus fits a different dynasty; most Egyptologists reject the revision. Critical scholars such as Israel Finkelstein and William Dever find no archaeological sign of a large exodus or conquest, and think Israel emerged from within Canaan, perhaps with a small group from Egypt.

The Hyksos, "rulers of foreign lands," were Semitic kings who ruled northern Egypt from Avaris (about 1650–1550 BC) until they were driven out by Ahmose. Manfred Bietak's excavations at Tell el-Dab'a showed a large Canaanite population there. The Egyptian priest Manetho (about 280 BC), quoted by Josephus in Against Apion 1, tells of shepherds expelled to Judea, where they built Jerusalem, and in another version of lepers led by a renegade priest Osarseph who took the name Moses. Josephus himself identified the Hyksos with Israel.

Most scholars see Manetho's stories as Egyptian anti-Jewish polemic, shaped partly by the Bible. But some, such as Donald Redford and Jan Assmann, think the memory of the Hyksos expulsion lies somewhere behind both Egyptian and Israelite traditions, an expulsion of Semites that Israel later remembered as a liberation. Defenders of the early or late date place the exodus well after the Hyksos, and do not identify them with Israel.

deep.h: Passover in Jewish and Christian practice
deep.b:
Jewish practice: After the Temple's fall in AD 70, the sacrifice ceased, and the home Seder took its place. The Haggadah, with roots in Mishnah Pesachim 10, moves through blessings, four cups of wine, the four questions asked by a child, the story of the exodus with its four sons and ten plagues, the songs of Hallel (Psalms 113–118), and closes with the hope "Next year in Jerusalem." Siegfried Stein showed how the Haggadah borrowed forms of the Greco-Roman symposium, and Baruch Bokser how the Seder answered the loss of the Temple after AD 70. Leaven is removed from homes, and matzah is eaten for the week.

Christian practice: Jesus' Last Supper with bread and cup took place at Passover; the Synoptic Gospels present it as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12), which Joachim Jeremias defended; John P. Meier and others follow John, who places Jesus' death at the hour when the lambs were slaughtered (John 19:14). Early Christians kept Pascha, Easter; some in Asia Minor (the Quartodecimans) kept it on the fourteenth of Nisan itself, and Melito of Sardis' homily On Pascha (about AD 165) reads Exodus 12 as a prophecy of Christ, and the Easter Vigil's Exsultet still sings "This is the night" of the Passover and the sea. Some Christian groups today hold "Christ in the Passover" meals; many Jews find this appropriation painful, a reminder that one festival now carries two meanings.

deep.title: A speculation: Passover as a protection rite, transformed
deep.b: The blood on doorposts, the night danger, the destroyer and the haste all fit an older protective rite, and the text does not hide this: it simply gives each element a new meaning tied to one historical night. I suspect that is the key to the chapter. Whatever its origins, Exodus turns a rite about warding off danger into a rite about memory and identity, which is why it survived when its sacrificial core ended in AD 70. This is my own reading, built on the critical view that Passover had earlier roots, and it is not provable.

echoes: Leviticus 23:5–8; Numbers 9:1–14; Deuteronomy 16:1–8; Joshua 5:10–11; 2 Kings 23:21–23; Ezra 6:19–22; Luke 22:7–20; John 19:31–36; 1 Corinthians 5:7–8; Hebrews 11:28; Jude 5

settings.what: The law of the Passover and Unleavened Bread
settings.to: Moses and Aaron in Egypt, to tell the whole assembly of Israel
settings.when: Before the last blow, in the month that becomes the first of the year
settings.why: To give Israel a calendar and a rite. It binds every household of Israel, by fathers' houses. In the seven days without yeast it binds the foreigner living among them as well (12:19). Each household takes a lamb on the tenth day and slaughters it at twilight on the fourteenth. They put its blood on the doorposts and eat it roasted with flat bread and bitter herbs, dressed for the road. Then for seven days no yeast may be eaten or kept in the house, on pain of being cut off. It answers the need for protection on the night of judgment.
settings.readers: For Israel the first Passover was kept in Egyptian homes, but the law made it a rule for all time, wherever Israel lived. The yearly meal makes every generation part of the exodus.
views: Traditional readers take the Passover and Unleavened Bread as given together in Egypt.
Many scholars think a shepherds' spring sacrifice and a farmers' barley festival were joined and tied to the exodus. They think the household form of the rite speaks to Israel without a temple.

settings.what: Moses' instructions to the elders
settings.to: All the elders of Israel
settings.when: The day of the first Passover
settings.why: To have the elders pick animals for their clans, mark the doorposts with hyssop and blood, and stay inside until morning, because the LORD will pass over. Moses adds how it is to be kept in the land. When the children ask what the service means, the parents will tell them.
settings.readers: For Israel the words made the elders and fathers the teachers of the story. The Haggadah of the Seder is built on such questions.

settings.what: Pharaoh's order to leave
settings.to: Moses and Aaron, summoned in the night
settings.when: After the death of the firstborn
settings.why: To drive them out with their flocks and herds, and to ask, "And bless me too." The proud king who asked "Who is this LORD?" now asks his slaves for a blessing.
settings.readers: For Israel this was the contest of 5:2 settled. Pharaoh's last words admit that blessing comes through the people he enslaved, as God promised Abraham (Genesis 12:3).

settings.what: The rule on who may eat the Passover
settings.to: Moses and Aaron
settings.when: As Israel leaves Egypt
settings.why: To say who may eat it. No foreigner or hired worker may, but a slave who has been circumcised may. So may a foreigner living among them who has all his males circumcised. One law holds for the one born in the land and the foreigner. The rule answers a real question, since a mixed crowd left Egypt with Israel (12:38).
settings.readers: For Israel the rule taught that belonging comes by covenant, not by birth alone. Outsiders could join the people of God.

traditions.q: The Last Supper was a Passover meal. Are Christ's body and blood present in the Lord's Supper?
views: Yes. The bread and wine become Christ's body and blood in substance, called transubstantiation, while looking and tasting the same (Catechism 1376). The Mass makes present Christ's one sacrifice as the Passover lamb (Catechism 1340, 1366–1367).
The bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood when the Holy Spirit is called down on them. The Orthodox call this a mystery and usually avoid explaining how it happens.

Christ's true body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine, and are given to all who eat (Augsburg Confession, article 10; Formula of Concord, article 7). The bread remains bread, and the Supper is a gift received, not a sacrifice offered.

Believers truly feed on Christ, but spiritually, as the Holy Spirit joins them to Christ in heaven; the bread and wine do not change (Calvin, Institutes 4.17; Westminster Confession 29.7). Zwingli, an early Reformed leader, stressed remembrance more.

Article 28 rejects transubstantiation and says Christ's body is given and eaten only in a heavenly and spiritual way, received by faith. Anglicans are divided: Anglo-Catholics hold a strong real presence, and evangelical Anglicans a view close to Calvin's.

The Lord's Supper is an ordinance, a symbolic act of obedience in which believers remember the Redeemer's death and look for his return (Baptist Faith and Message, article 7). It is a memorial, as Passover was a memorial of the exodus.

title: The Long Way Round
sum: God claims every firstborn in Israel, human and animal. Moses tells the people to remember the day they came out of the house of slaves: keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread each year in the month of Abib, tell their children why, and wear it "as a sign on your hand and a reminder between your eyes." Firstborn animals are to be given to the LORD and firstborn sons ransomed.

God does not lead Israel by the short coastal road through Philistine land, for fear that war would send them back to Egypt. Instead they go by the wilderness road toward the Sea of Reeds, armed and in order. Moses carries Joseph's bones, as Joseph had made Israel swear. From Succoth to Etham the LORD goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.
readings: Read as memory
The chapter turns the exodus into lasting practice: a yearly feast, the redemption of firstborn, teaching children, and signs worn on the body. Remembering becomes the work of every generation.
Read as guidance
God chooses a longer road for the people's good, knowing their weakness. Readers have often applied this to spiritual life: the shortest way is not always the best way.
Read as geography
The road of the Philistines along the coast was guarded by Egyptian forts; the wilderness road southeast avoided them. The route matters for where the sea crossing happened.

views.H: Israel avoided the fortified coastal road and went south or southeast. The pillar was a real, visible sign of God's presence.
views.M: An escaping group would naturally avoid the fortified Ways of Horus. The cloud and fire may preserve the memory of a desert guide or a sacred standard.
views.C: 13:1–16 is a later instruction (Deuteronomistic in style) linking the firstborn and unleavened bread to the exodus. The mention of the Philistines shows a writer after 1175 BC. The pillar of cloud is a literary image shared by J and P.
views.J: Tefillin are based on 13:9 and 13:16, and their boxes contain 13:1–10 and 13:11–16 along with Deuteronomy 6:4–9 and 11:13–21. Moses' care for Joseph's bones is praised in the Talmud (Sotah 13a). The ceremony of pidyon ha-ben is kept to this day.
views.X: Jesus was presented at the Temple as a firstborn (Luke 2:22–23). Paul says Israel was "baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Corinthians 10:1–2), and the church fathers read the pillar as Christ, light for the people of God (John 8:12).

echoes: 12:14–20; 34:18–20; Numbers 3:11–13; Numbers 9:15–23; Deuteronomy 6:8; Joshua 24:32; Luke 2:22–23; 1 Corinthians 10:1–2; Hebrews 11:22

settings.what: The law of the firstborn and the feast of remembrance
settings.by: The LORD to Moses, then Moses
settings.to: Moses; then the people of Israel, just out of Egypt
settings.when: The day they come out
settings.why: God claims every firstborn of humans and animals as his own, having spared Israel's firstborn on the night of judgment. Moses passes it on with the feast. Keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread each year in the month of Abib. Give every firstborn male animal to the LORD, ransom every firstborn son, and tell your son why. It binds every Israelite household once they live in Canaan, "a land flowing with milk and honey." The words answer a problem of time: how a people will remember a rescue its children did not see.
settings.readers: For Israel the firstborn sons ransomed in every family were a living reminder of the night in Egypt. Jewish tradition took 13:9 and 13:16 as the source of tefillin, the prayer boxes worn on the hand and head.

title: Through the Sea
sum: God has Israel turn back and camp by the sea, to make Pharaoh think they are lost. Pharaoh, regretting his decision, chases them with six hundred elite chariots and all Egypt's chariotry. Trapped between army and sea, the Israelites panic and blame Moses. Moses answers: "Do not be afraid... The LORD will fight for you. And you? You will keep quiet."

The angel of God and the pillar of cloud move behind Israel, darkness for Egypt and light for Israel. Moses stretches his hand over the sea, and a fierce east wind blows all night, turning the sea to dry ground with water like walls on either side. Israel crosses. The Egyptians follow; God throws them into panic, their chariot wheels fail, and at dawn the sea returns. "Not one of them was left." Israel sees the great hand of the LORD, fears him, and believes in the LORD and in Moses his servant.
readings: Read as miracle

The defining saving act of the Old Testament: God split the sea for his people and destroyed the army of the world's greatest power. Later psalms and prophets return to it again and again (Psalm 106:9–12; Isaiah 51:10).
Read as natural event guided by God
A strong east wind over a shallow body of water can drive it back; Drews and Han's model and similar studies show how. Many believers see God's power in the timing and outcome.
Read as myth and theology

The sea is the ancient symbol of chaos, and the story pictures God's victory over it as a new creation. Isaiah 51:9–10 joins the creation battle with the crossing. Critical readers see two sources: in one, a wind dries the sea and the Egyptians are thrown into panic; in the other, the sea splits at Moses' command.

views.H: Israel crossed a real body of water, the Gulf of Suez or a lake on Egypt's eastern border, and the Egyptian chariot force drowned. Hoffmeier locates the crossing near the Ballah Lake or Lake Timsah; others prefer the Gulf of Aqaba.
views.M: A small group escaped Egyptian pursuers, perhaps through marshland where chariots bogged down. The story grew in the telling into the splitting of a sea.
views.C: Two accounts combined: J (God drives the sea back by a wind all night; the Egyptians panic and are drowned at dawn) and P (Moses stretches his hand, the waters split and stand as walls, Israel walks through). Neither can be located; the story is Israel's foundational victory myth.
views.J: The Midrash describes ten miracles at the sea and twelve paths for twelve tribes. Nahshon jumped in first. The Talmud says God rebuked the angels for singing as the Egyptians drowned: "My creatures are drowning, and you would sing?" (Megillah 10b). The crossing is remembered on the seventh day of Passover.
views.X: Paul calls the crossing a baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–2), and the church reads it at the Easter Vigil. Hebrews 11:29 praises Israel's faith. The fathers saw the drowned Egyptians as sins destroyed in the water of baptism (Origen, Gregory of Nyssa).

deep.h: Where was the Sea of Reeds?
deep.b:
Exodus names Pi-hahiroth, Migdol and Baal-zephon (14:2), but none is certainly located. Scholars propose:

Lake Sirbonis (Lake Bardawil), a lagoon along the Mediterranean coast, near a shrine of Baal-zephon at Mount Casius (Otto Eissfeldt). But it lies on the Way of the Philistines that God avoided. Lake Ballah or Lake Timsah, reedy lakes on the line of the modern Suez Canal, near the border forts. James Hoffmeier's work on an ancient eastern Delta coastline and lagoon system supports this area. The Bitter Lakes or the Gulf of Suez, the traditional site, consistent with the Septuagint's "Red Sea" and with Numbers 33:10–11, where Israel camps by Yam Suf after leaving the crossing. The Gulf of Aqaba, which 1 Kings 9:26 clearly calls Yam Suf, favored by those who put Mount Sinai in Arabia (Galatians 4:25), such as Colin Humphreys.

Bernard Batto argued that Yam Suf also had a cosmic sense, the "sea at the end" of the world. Many critical scholars think the tradition never had a precise location in view.

echoes: Numbers 33:5–8; Joshua 2:10; Joshua 4:23; Nehemiah 9:9–11; Psalm 77:16–20; Psalm 106:7–12; Psalm 136:13–15; Isaiah 43:16–17; Isaiah 51:10; 1 Corinthians 10:1–2; Hebrews 11:29; Joshua 24:5–7; Psalm 66:6; Psalm 78:13; Psalm 114:1–8; Jude 5

settings.what: The people's complaint and Moses' answer
settings.to: Moses; then the Israelites
settings.when: When they see Pharaoh's chariots coming and are trapped against the sea
settings.why: The terrified people cry out and blame Moses: were there no graves in Egypt? They say, "Serving Egypt is better for us than dying in the wilderness." Moses turns panic into trust: "Do not be afraid. Take your stand, and see how the LORD will save you today." The LORD will fight for them, and they will keep quiet.
settings.readers: For Israel the crossing became the model of rescue by God alone, sung in later psalms. Exiles who hoped for a new exodus recalled it (Isaiah 43:16–19). The complaint also began a pattern of longing for Egypt that runs through the wilderness stories.

title: The Song of the Sea
sum: Moses and Israel sing: "I will sing to the LORD, for he has risen up high, so high. Horse and its rider he has flung into the sea." The poem celebrates the LORD as warrior and king. It pictures the waters piled up by the breath of his nostrils and the enemy sinking like lead, and asks, "Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?" Then it looks ahead: the nations tremble as God leads his people to his holy mountain, where he will reign forever. Miriam the prophet leads the women in dance and sings the refrain.

Three days into the wilderness of Shur, the people find only bitter water at Marah and grumble. God shows Moses a piece of wood that makes the water sweet, gives a rule and a test, and promises: "I am the LORD, your healer." They camp at Elim, with twelve springs and seventy palms.
readings: Read as ancient poetry

Many scholars count the Song among the oldest Hebrew poems. Its archaic grammar, short lines and Canaanite imagery suggest it was sung long before the prose story was written. Its text is laid out in a special pattern in Torah scrolls.
Read as worship

The Song is the Bible's first hymn. The whole Song (Az Yashir, 15:1–18) is recited every morning in the opening psalms of Jewish prayer (Pesukei de-Zimra), and verses 11 and 18 are part of the blessing after the Shema, morning and evening. It is also read in synagogue on the Sabbath of Song (Shabbat Shirah) and on the seventh day of Passover. Christians sing it as a canticle, above all at the Easter Vigil.
Read as the turn to the wilderness
Right after the song, the people complain. Marah's bitter water begins the wilderness stories, where the people saved at the sea must learn to trust day by day.

views.H: Moses composed the song at the sea, and Miriam led the women's response. The look ahead to the nations and the sanctuary is prophecy.
views.M: The short Song of Miriam (15:21) may be one of the oldest memories of Israel, a victory chant sung by a group that escaped Egypt. The longer Song grew from it.
views.C: Scholars divide. Cross and Freedman dated the Song to the 1100s BC; others to the time of Solomon's Temple (15:17) or later, with deliberately archaic style. All agree it originally stood alone and was later set into the prose.
views.J: The Mekhilta says that at the sea even a maidservant saw more than the prophet Ezekiel, and that the song was sung by all Israel in response, phrase by phrase. The rabbis read the future tense "then Moses will sing" (az yashir) as a hint of the resurrection (Talmud, Sanhedrin 91b).
views.X: In Revelation 15:3 the victors sing "the song of God's servant Moses and the song of the Lamb" by a sea of glass. The fathers read the sweetened water of Marah as the cross, which makes the bitterness of life sweet. The Song of Moses is a canticle in Christian liturgy.

deep.h: Dating the Song of the Sea
deep.b:
Early: In 1955 Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman argued that the Song's grammar is archaic: verbs in the old short form with past meaning, the ending -mo for "them," old relative zu (15:13, 16), and the repetitive style of Ugaritic poetry. They dated it to the 1100s BC, making it one of the oldest poems in the Bible, perhaps older than the prose story. Brian Russell (2007) defends an early date and argues the Song shaped later accounts of the crossing.

Later: Other scholars think the "mountain of your inheritance" and "sanctuary" in 15:17 point to Jerusalem and the Temple, which would date the poem after Solomon; some regard archaic forms as deliberate poetic style. Martin Noth and others suggested that Miriam's short song (15:21) is the original and the longer Song developed from it.

Traditional: Jews and Christians take the Song as Moses' own composition, sung on the shore. The future-looking verses (15:14–17) are read as prophecy, fulfilled in the conquest and the Temple.

deep.title: A speculation: why the Song does not mention the walls
deep.b: The poem has waters "heaped up" and "standing like a mound," but no people walking between walls of water: the focus is entirely on the drowning of the enemy. If the Song is older than the prose, it may preserve the earliest form of the memory: Egypt's army was destroyed at the sea by the LORD's wind. The crossing on dry ground may have been made explicit by later tellers. The observation goes back to Martin Noth and George Coats and is discussed by Childs; my part is only the suggestion about which form came first, and it cannot be proved; the Song's silence might simply reflect a poem's choice of subject.

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:1–43; Judges 5:1–31; 1 Samuel 18:6–7; Psalm 77:16–20; Psalm 118:14; Isaiah 12:2; Isaiah 51:9–11; Revelation 15:2–4

settings.what: The Song of the Sea
settings.to: The LORD, in the hearing of the whole people
settings.when: On the far shore, right after the crossing
settings.why: To praise the LORD as warrior and king. Horse and rider he has flung into the sea, the waters stood up at the breath of his nostrils, and no god is like him. Then the song looks ahead: the nations tremble, the people are brought to God's holy mountain and sanctuary, and he reigns forever.
settings.readers: For Israel the song taught it to tell its rescue as worship. It is recited every morning in the synagogue. Its look ahead to Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan, and to a sanctuary, may show that it was sung in the land.
views: Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman dated its old Hebrew to the 1100s BC or earlier, among the oldest poems in the Bible. More recently Brian Russell has argued that 15:1–21 is one early poem from about the mid-1100s BC.
Other scholars date it to the time of the kings or later, reading the holy mountain as Zion and its Temple.
Traditional readers take it as sung by Moses and Israel at the sea, with the mountain as Sinai or the land itself.

settings.what: Miriam's song
settings.to: The Israelites who sang with Moses ("them," masculine in Hebrew), while the women follow her with drums and dancing
settings.when: At the sea, answering the song
settings.why: To lead the refrain: sing to the LORD, for he has risen up high; horse and rider he has flung into the sea. Her words answer and repeat the opening line of the song (15:1).
settings.readers: For Israel women's victory songs were a custom (1 Samuel 18:6–7), and Miriam was remembered as a leader sent with Moses and Aaron (Micah 6:4). Many scholars think her short song is the oldest core of the whole poem.

settings.what: The decree at Marah
settings.to: The Israelites, three days into the wilderness
settings.when: After the bitter water is made sweet
settings.why: To set a rule and a ruling, and a promise. If Israel listens to the LORD and keeps his laws, he will not put on them the sickness he put on Egypt, "For I am the LORD, your healer." It binds the whole people from their first days in the wilderness, before Sinai. It answers their first complaint.
settings.readers: For Israel the lesson was that the God who made bitter water sweet can heal. Obedience and health were tied together from the start.
